## Observations

1. Every move merges the contents of two bags without splitting any original bag’s stones. Thus the nonempty final bags correspond to a partition of the original bag indices, and every such partition is reachable by merging each group into one of its own bags.
2. A partition’s XOR is the XOR of its group sums; empty bags contribute zero. Different partitions can produce the same XOR, so the answer counts distinct XOR values rather than partitions.
3. In any partition of the remaining indices, exactly one group contains the smallest remaining index. Choosing that group first gives a unique order in which to enumerate the groups.
4. A bitmask can represent a group, and its stone sum can be computed from the sum of the mask with one bit removed. With \(N\le 12\), there are at most \(2^{12}\) masks and \(B_{12}=4{,}213{,}597\) partitions, where \(B_N\) is the \(N\)th Bell number.

## Solution sketch

1. > A bitmask can represent a group, and its stone sum can be computed from the sum of the mask with one bit removed. With \(N\le 12\), there are at most \(2^{12}\) masks and \(B_{12}=4{,}213{,}597\) partitions, where \(B_N\) is the \(N\)th Bell number.
   
   Read the stone counts and precompute the sum for every mask. Set the empty mask’s sum to zero. For each nonempty mask, remove its lowest set bit and add the corresponding bag’s count to the already computed sum of the smaller mask.

2. > In any partition of the remaining indices, exactly one group contains the smallest remaining index. Choosing that group first gives a unique order in which to enumerate the groups.
   
   Start a depth-first search with all indices remaining and a running XOR of zero. At each nonempty state, pick the lowest set bit of the remaining mask. Enumerate every submask of the other remaining bits, including the empty submask, and attach the chosen bit to form the next group. Recurse after removing that group and XORing its precomputed sum into the running value. Including the empty submask allows singleton groups; choosing all other bits allows all remaining bags to form one group.

3. > A partition’s XOR is the XOR of its group sums; empty bags contribute zero. Different partitions can produce the same XOR, so the answer counts distinct XOR values rather than partitions.
   
   When no indices remain, insert the running XOR into a set, even if it is zero. Use indices rather than stone counts to identify bags, so equal input counts need no special handling. After the search, print the set’s size.

4. > Every move merges the contents of two bags without splitting any original bag’s stones. Thus the nonempty final bags correspond to a partition of the original bag indices, and every such partition is reachable by merging each group into one of its own bags.
   
   This correspondence makes the enumeration exhaustive: the singleton partition represents doing nothing, the one-group partition represents merging everything, and every other partition gives a reachable result. The search has \(B_N\) leaves. A node with one remaining index has exactly one child, which is a leaf; every other internal node has at least two children. Thus there are \(O(B_N)\) search nodes, and each submask choice generates one search edge. The expected time is \(O(2^N+B_N)\) with hash-set insertion, and the space is \(O(2^N+N+D)\), where \(D\) is the number of distinct XOR values stored.
